hook: A long, multi-page file that starts as a cold containment document and slowly becomes something far more personal. The page opens with a content warning covering transphobia, gender dysphoria, bullying, abuse and suicide, and those themes are handled with care rather than for shock. Read the pages in order, and keep track of who gets called by a name and who is reduced to a number.
whyItMatters: Its anomaly is almost purely benevolent, so the conflict comes entirely from the Foundation's reflex to hide anything unusual. Tagged as both lgbtq and bittersweet, it writes about trans experience through a young narrator who is guarded, foul-mouthed and very funny in believable ways. It also hands the Ethics Committee an uncomfortable role, since the same office that keeps the girl in custody for her own good is the one that insists on distance between researcher and subject.
thingsToNotice:
Watch the interview logs change register: the early transcripts are flat and procedural, and by the middle Dr. Park and the girl are trading stories about abusive parents and laughing together. When she finally names Little Caribou Lake, the O5 Council votes down Park's proposal to declassify it, and he has to tell her the promise to protect the lake is broken. The links that move you between revisions are part of the plot, so each update shows what the institution decided while the characters were talking.

The unsent draft email reading only that it was envy reframes the earlier conversation about gender envy: Park was trans too, and vanished from a locked office the day the injunction arrived because SCP-6113-1 came for her. In the last revision she returns as Janet, the entity breaks the girl out of Site-17 while non-lethal rounds bounce harmlessly off them, and the farewell letters are signed Janet Park and Chloe Park. Meanwhile the fenced-off lake receives no visitors, transitions keep happening everywhere else, and the Foundation is left wondering whether the lake was ever anomalous at all.

related.note: Named in the description as the comparison point for this bodily change, which here is noted to be painless.
